chapters.title: Chapter 4: India's Position in the New Trade Order

lessons.title: Sectoral Winners on NSE and BSE: Defence, Chemicals, Textiles and Electronics Manufacturing

children.text: Everything this course has covered so far, trade rerouting, friendshoring, PLI schemes, is a macro story until you translate it into names you can actually find on NSE and BSE. This lesson does that translation across four sectors: defence, specialty chemicals, textiles and electronics manufacturing services. Not every sector tells the same success story, and a sharp analyst needs to be honest about which ones are genuinely riding this structural shift versus which ones are lagging behind a narrative that has gotten ahead of the data.

body.text: A macro theme is not automatically a stock-picking edge. Defence and chemicals show what a genuine structural tailwind looks like in listed company numbers. Textiles shows what it looks like when the tailwind has not actually arrived yet, no matter how often the theme gets discussed.

children.text: Defence: Import Substitution First, Exports Second

India's defence sector is driven mainly by a domestic story, phased "positive indigenisation lists" that progressively ban the import of specific defence items, forcing the Ministry of Defence's own orders toward Indian manufacturers. The export side has grown from a genuinely small base but at a striking pace: government figures put India's defence exports at roughly ₹21,000 crore, close to $2.6 billion, in FY24, up from close to ₹1,900 crore in FY17, an increase of roughly tenfold or more over seven years. NSE launched a dedicated Nifty India Defence index in 2023, tracking listed names including Hindustan Aeronautics, Bharat Electronics, Bharat Dynamics, Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Cochin Shipyard and private players like Solar Industries and Bharat Forge.

body.label: India's defence exports, FY17 to FY24
body.context: Government-reported figures; roughly a tenfold or greater increase, driven primarily by domestic indigenisation policy rather than global China+1 dynamics directly.

body.text: Defence is worth including in this lesson precisely because it is different from the other three sectors: its growth is driven mainly by India's own strategic autonomy push, not by global companies actively diversifying supply chains toward India. It connects to this course's broader theme, rising geopolitical fragmentation, without being a direct China+1 trade story.

children.text: Specialty Chemicals: The Quiet China+1 Winner

Specialty chemicals has been a genuinely direct China+1 beneficiary, and one that gets far less attention than electronics. China's own environmental crackdowns from around 2017 onward shut down large numbers of polluting chemical plants, creating supply gaps and price volatility that pushed global agrochemical and pharmaceutical majors to qualify a second source. Indian companies, SRF in fluorochemicals, Aarti Industries and Navin Fluorine in specialty and fluorine chemistry, and PI Industries in custom synthesis for global agrochemical companies, have won multi-year supply agreements from clients that explicitly cite supply chain diversification as a reason for the shift, not just cost.

children.text: Textiles: The Sector Where the Narrative Has Outrun the Data

This is where an honest analyst has to push back on the popular story. India launched a PLI scheme for man-made fibre and technical textiles in 2021, with an outlay of roughly ₹10,683 crore, aimed explicitly at capturing garment export share shifting away from China. So far, the results are underwhelming relative to the ambition. India's apparel exports run at roughly $16 billion a year, while Bangladesh, a far smaller economy, exports more than $40 billion of ready-made garments annually. Vietnam has also continued gaining apparel export share faster than India through the same period this course has documented China+1 activity elsewhere.

body.text: If a sector has a plausible China+1 story, a government PLI scheme and years of media coverage but its actual global export share has barely moved, that gap is the single most useful signal in this entire lesson. It tells you the theme and the fundamentals have decoupled, which is exactly the situation a sharp investor should be most suspicious of, not most excited about.

children.text: Electronics Manufacturing Services: The Direct Listed Proxy

Dixon Technologies is the clearest listed proxy for the electronics story covered in the previous lesson, a contract manufacturer that expanded from LED TVs and washing machines into mobile phone assembly under the PLI framework, re-rating sharply as its order book diversified across brands. Amber Enterprises, Kaynes Technology and Syrma SGS have followed a similar playbook across consumer durables and industrial electronics. The risk with this group is precisely the flip side of its appeal: much of the future growth global investors expect from India's electronics build-out is often already reflected in these companies' valuations, which is why checking a stock's price-to-earnings multiple against its actual revenue growth on a tool like screener.in matters as much as confirming the underlying macro story is real.

body.title: Before you buy the theme, check the company
steps: Confirm what share of revenue actually comes from exports or from clients explicitly diversifying away from China, versus purely domestic demand
Check customer concentration: a single large client, like one global smartphone brand, creates real dependency risk
Compare revenue growth over the last 3 to 5 years against the stock's current valuation multiple on screener.in, rather than assuming the theme justifies any price
Read recent management commentary or concall transcripts for specific capacity expansion or new client wins, not just references to the broader trend
For sectors like textiles, verify actual export or market share data has moved, not just that a policy scheme or news narrative exists

body.title: Judge the sector
body.question: A sector has an active PLI scheme, frequent media coverage of China+1 potential, and a government minister citing it in speeches. Its actual global export market share has been flat for three years. Based on this lesson, how should an analyst weigh this sector against one with rising export share but far less media attention?
options: Favour the sector with more media coverage, since attention usually precedes fundamentals
Treat both equally, since PLI schemes guarantee eventual success regardless of current data
Favour the sector with rising export share, and treat the heavily discussed but stagnant sector with real scepticism until the data actually moves
Ignore export share entirely and focus only on the size of the PLI outlay announced
body.explanation: This lesson's textiles case is exactly this pattern: narrative and policy activity without matching data movement. The specialty chemicals case shows the opposite, real data with comparatively less mainstream attention. Data should always outrank narrative volume when the two disagree.

cards.definition: A phased list of defence items India's Ministry of Defence commits to procuring only from domestic manufacturers, banning their import after a set date.
Companies that manufacture electronic products, such as phones or appliances, on contract for brand owners, without owning the underlying product design themselves.

A situation where a sector receives heavy policy and media attention around a structural theme, but its actual output, export or market share data has not moved to match, a signal for caution rather than excitement.

points: India's defence exports rose roughly tenfold or more from FY17 to FY24, but the sector is driven mainly by domestic indigenisation policy, not direct China+1 trade dynamics.

Specialty chemicals is a genuine, data-backed China+1 winner, with companies like SRF, Aarti Industries and PI Industries winning supply agreements explicitly framed around diversification from China.
Textiles has the policy support and the media narrative but not yet the data: India's apparel exports remain far below Bangladesh's, despite years of China+1 discussion.

Electronics manufacturing services companies like Dixon Technologies are the most direct listed proxies for India's PLI-driven electronics story, but valuations often already price in a large share of expected future growth.

The single most useful diagnostic in this lesson is the gap, or lack of one, between a sector's narrative and its actual export or market share data, and that gap should drive scepticism or confidence more than headlines do.
Any company mentioned in this lesson is an illustrative example of a sectoral theme, not a recommendation, and requires its own full valuation and fundamental analysis before any investment decision.
